q: About how fast does sound travel through air at room temperature?
x: Sound travels at about 343 meters per second at 20 C, which is why you hear thunder several seconds after seeing lightning.

q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
x: Carbon has six protons. Its ability to form four bonds makes it the backbone of all known life.

q: Which gas makes up most of the thin atmosphere of Mars?
x: About 95 percent of Mars's atmosphere is carbon dioxide, but the air is so thin that pressure is under 1 percent of Earth's.

q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
x: K comes from kalium, the Latin form of an Arabic word for plant ashes, the original source of potassium compounds.

q: Who published the Sun-centered model of the solar system in 1543?
x: Copernicus's book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was published in the year he died.

q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 C?
x: A pH of 7 is neutral. Lower values are acidic and higher values are basic.

q: Which part of a plant cell carries out photosynthesis?
x: Chloroplasts are thought to descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancient cell.

q: What is the SI unit of energy?
x: The joule is named after English physicist James Prescott Joule. One joule is roughly the energy needed to lift an apple one meter.

q: What are the blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart called?
x: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the high pressure of each heartbeat.

q: Which planet has a day that is longer than its year?
x: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backward.

q: Who created the first widely accepted periodic table in 1869?
x: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and correctly predicted the properties of gallium and germanium.

q: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for balance and coordination?
x: The cerebellum is only about a tenth of the brain's volume but holds more than half of its neurons.

q: Which hormone, made in the pancreas, lowers blood sugar?
x: People with type 1 diabetes cannot make enough insulin and must replace it, as first done in 1922.

q: What is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust?
x: Aluminum was once more valuable than gold because it was so hard to extract, until an electrolysis method was found in 1886.

q: Which scale ranks minerals by hardness from 1 to 10?
x: Friedrich Mohs created the scale in 1812. A fingernail scratches talc, but only a diamond scratches a diamond.

q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
x: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

q: Who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610?
x: These moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, are still called the Galilean moons.

q: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
x: Pb comes from plumbum, the Latin word for lead, which is also the root of the word plumber.

q: What type of chemical bond involves atoms sharing pairs of electrons?
x: The two hydrogen atoms in an H2 molecule are held together by a single shared pair of electrons.

q: What is the SI unit of frequency?
x: One hertz is one cycle per second. It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who first proved the existence of radio waves.

q: What does a Geiger counter detect?
x: A Geiger counter clicks each time a particle of radiation ionizes the gas inside its tube.

q: Which monk is known as the father of modern genetics for his experiments on pea plants?
x: Mendel worked in the 1860s, but his findings on inheritance were largely ignored until around 1900.

q: A deficiency of which nutrient can cause night blindness?
x: Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the pigment in the eye that works in dim light. Carrots and sweet potatoes are good sources.

q: What is the main component of natural gas?
x: Methane has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms (CH4). Natural gas has no smell, so a harmless odor is added for safety.

q: What is the common name for sodium bicarbonate?
x: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with acid, which makes cakes and breads rise.

q: What does a light-year measure?
x: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers.

q: Which scientist discovered the electron in 1897?
x: Thomson's cathode ray experiments showed that atoms contain smaller, negatively charged particles.

q: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
x: We inherit 23 chromosomes from each parent, making 23 pairs in total.

q: Which layer at the back of the eye detects light and sends signals to the brain?
x: The retina holds about 120 million rod cells for dim light and about 6 million cone cells for color.

q: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
x: At absolute zero, 0 kelvin, particles have the lowest possible energy. Nothing in nature has been cooled to exactly that point.

q: Which planet spins on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees?
x: Uranus's odd tilt means each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

q: What type of wave is sound in air?
x: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate back and forth along the direction the wave travels. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

q: Which element has the chemical symbol Sn?
x: Sn comes from stannum, the Latin word for tin. Tin mixed with copper makes bronze.

q: Which organ produces bile to help digest fats?
x: The liver makes bile, and the gallbladder stores and concentrates it. The liver also has a remarkable ability to regrow.

q: On which planet is Olympus Mons, the tallest known volcano in the solar system?
x: Olympus Mons is about 22 km tall, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level.

q: What is the scientific study of earthquakes called?
x: Seismologists also use earthquake waves to map Earth's interior, which is how the liquid outer core was discovered.

q: Which scale is used to classify hurricanes by wind speed?
x: The Saffir-Simpson scale has five categories, and Category 5 means sustained winds of at least 157 mph.

q: Which element makes up pure diamonds and graphite?
x: Diamond and graphite differ only in how their carbon atoms are arranged. Graphite is soft enough to write with.

q: What instrument measures wind speed?
x: Most anemometers use spinning cups. The first one was described by Leon Battista Alberti around 1450.

q: Which English physician described the circulation of blood in 1628?
x: Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood in a loop around the body, overturning ideas that dated back to ancient Greece.

q: Which large spiral galaxy is the nearest major galaxy to the Milky Way?
x: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away and is moving toward us. It is expected to merge with the Milky Way in billions of years.

q: Which Apollo mission made the first crewed Moon landing?
x: Apollo 11 landed in July 1969, and the astronauts spent about 21 hours on the surface.

q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
x: The ohm is named after Georg Ohm, who showed that current is proportional to voltage in a conductor.

q: What are the two main metals in Earth's core?
x: The solid inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, around 5,000 to 6,000 C.

q: Which noble gas has the chemical symbol Ar?
x: Argon makes up almost 1 percent of Earth's air. Its name comes from the Greek word for lazy, because it barely reacts.

q: In computing, what does RAM stand for?
x: RAM is a computer's short-term working memory, and its contents are lost when the power is switched off.

q: Who is often called the first computer programmer for her notes on the Analytical Engine?
x: In 1843 Lovelace published an algorithm meant for Charles Babbage's machine, which was never completed in his lifetime.

q: How many bits are in one byte?
x: A single byte can represent 256 different values, enough for one letter in the ASCII character set.

q: What is the chemical formula of ozone?
x: Ozone is made of three oxygen atoms. Near the ground it is a pollutant, but high up it shields us from ultraviolet light.

q: In which cell structures are proteins assembled?
x: Ribosomes read messenger RNA and link amino acids together in the correct order. A human cell can contain millions of them.

q: What is the largest artery in the human body?
x: The aorta is about as wide as a garden hose and carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the body.

q: Which component of blood is most important for clotting?
x: Platelets are tiny cell fragments that stick together at a wound to form a plug.

q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
x: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, so light from it takes over four years to reach us.

q: Marble is an example of which type of rock?
x: Marble forms when limestone is changed by intense heat and pressure deep in the Earth.

q: Which physicist is known for the uncertainty principle of quantum mechanics?
x: Heisenberg's 1927 principle says you cannot know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle at the same time.

q: What is the bending of light as it passes from air into water called?
x: Refraction is why a straw in a glass of water appears bent and why lenses can focus light.

q: Which isotope is used to date ancient organic remains up to about 50,000 years old?
x: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, so after roughly 50,000 years too little remains to measure accurately.

q: The thyroid and adrenal glands belong to which body system?
x: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate growth, metabolism and mood.

q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid?
x: Dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, sublimes at room pressure, which is why it leaves no puddle.

q: Which nonmetal element is liquid at room temperature?
x: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature and normal pressure. Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid with a sharp smell.

q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
x: Enamel is about 96 percent mineral. It cannot regrow because it contains no living cells.

q: Which French physicist discovered radioactivity in 1896?
x: Becquerel noticed that uranium salts fogged photographic plates even without light. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize with the Curies.

q: Which planet is the least dense, with an average density lower than water?
x: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm3, so in theory it would float in a bathtub big enough to hold it.

q: What is the SI base unit of temperature?
x: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so it has no negative values.

q: Which gas gives rotten eggs their smell?
x: Humans can smell hydrogen sulfide at extremely low concentrations, but at high levels it dulls the sense of smell and is toxic.

q: Which type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
x: The Milky Way has a bar of stars across its center, and the Sun lies in one of its spiral arms.

q: What was the name of the supercontinent that existed about 300 million years ago?
x: Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago, and the pieces slowly drifted into today's continents.

q: Who proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912?
x: Wegener was dismissed for decades because he could not explain the mechanism, but plate tectonics later proved him right.

q: Which layer of the Earth is made of liquid metal?
x: Swirling motion in the liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field.

q: Which instrument measures the amount of moisture in the air?
x: The hair hygrometer works because human hair gets slightly longer in humid air.

q: What primarily causes the seasons on Earth?
x: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

q: Which scientist discovered the neutron in 1932?
x: Chadwick won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. Neutrons became the key to nuclear fission.

q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
x: One pascal is a very small pressure, about the weight of a sheet of paper lying flat on a table.

q: What is the process of cell division that produces two identical body cells?
x: Mitosis is how you grow and heal wounds, while meiosis is the special division that makes sex cells.

q: Which blood type is considered the universal red cell donor?
x: O negative red cells lack the A, B and Rh markers, so they can usually be given to anyone in an emergency.

q: What is the visible surface layer of the Sun called?
x: The photosphere is about 5,500 C. The corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, is paradoxically millions of degrees hotter.

q: What type of star is our Sun?
x: Our Sun is a main-sequence star that is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its lifetime.

q: Which gas is the second most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?
x: Early Earth had almost no free oxygen. It built up after bacteria began photosynthesizing more than 2 billion years ago.

q: What name is given to the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion?
x: Inertia is why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly. Newton's first law describes it.

q: What does the abbreviation LED stand for?
x: LEDs turn electricity into light far more efficiently than old incandescent bulbs, which waste most of their energy as heat.

q: What does HTTP stand for in web addresses?
x: HTTP defines how browsers request pages from servers. The secure version, HTTPS, encrypts the connection.

q: Which astronomer discovered the three laws of planetary motion?
x: Kepler's first law showed that planets move in ellipses, not perfect circles. He built his laws from Brahe's precise observations.

q: Which molecule carries genetic instructions from DNA to the ribosomes?
x: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is the copy of a gene that ribosomes read to build a protein.

q: Which mineral is the main component of bones and teeth?
x: About 99 percent of the calcium in your body is stored in your bones and teeth.

q: What is the process by which plants release water vapor from their leaves?
x: A large tree can release hundreds of liters of water into the air on a hot day through tiny leaf pores called stomata.

q: In which organ does most nutrient absorption take place?
x: The small intestine is about 6 meters long, and its folded lining gives it a surface area of roughly a tennis court.

q: Around which planet does the moon Europa orbit?
x: Europa has an ice shell covering a salty ocean that may hold twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

q: What is the SI unit of power?
x: One watt equals one joule per second. The unit honors James Watt, who improved the steam engine.

q: Which two scientists proposed the double helix structure of DNA in 1953?
x: Their model drew on X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins's group.

q: What is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter?
x: Ceres is about 940 km across and holds roughly a third of the belt's total mass.

q: Which type of cloud is thin, wispy and found high in the sky?
x: Cirrus clouds are made of ice crystals and often appear before a change in the weather.

q: What is the Sun's thin outer atmosphere, visible during a total solar eclipse, called?
x: The corona is over a million degrees, far hotter than the Sun's surface, and scientists are still studying why.

q: A magnifying glass uses what kind of lens?
x: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and bends light rays together to a focus.

q: Which protein in red blood cells carries oxygen?
x: Each hemoglobin molecule can bind four oxygen molecules, and it contains iron.

q: What form of energy does a moving object have?
x: Kinetic energy equals one half of mass times speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples it.

q: What is the region around Earth dominated by its magnetic field called?
x: The magnetosphere deflects most of the solar wind and is why we see auroras near the poles.

q: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
x: Table salt is sodium chloride, made of sodium and chlorine.

q: Which particle in an atom has a negative electric charge?
x: Electrons carry a negative charge, protons a positive one, and neutrons none.

q: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion?
x: Newton published his laws of motion in 1687 in the Principia.

q: What is the pH of pure water at room temperature?
x: A pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.
